hypotheses.title: BridgeTester updateRollupAddress has no access control
hypotheses.description: In `BridgeTester.sol`, `updateRollupAddress(IOwnable _rollup)` is declared `external` with no modifier, unlike `AbsBridge.updateRollupAddress` which is `onlyRollupOrOwner`. Any external caller can set `rollup` to an arbitrary contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker calls `updateRollupAddress(attackerControlledContract)`. Then `onlyRollupOrOwner` checks `rollup.owner()` which the attacker's contract returns as the attacker, granting the attacker the ability to call `setSequencerInbox`, `setDelayedInbox`, `setOutbox` and register malicious inboxes/outboxes.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can register a malicious outbox to drain escrowed ETH/tokens via `executeCall` and inject messages into the delayed accumulator via a malicious inbox.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `onlyRollupOrOwner` (or `onlyDelegated` plus owner) modifier to `updateRollupAddress`.

hypotheses.title: AbsBoldStakingPool allows early withdrawal leaving pool underfunded for stake
hypotheses.description: The pool allows any depositor to withdraw their full deposit at any time, even after the pool has committed its stake to the rollup/challenge manager via `createAssertion`/`createEdge`. The comment acknowledges this is "okay" because the protocol move will still be created once the required stake is reached, but if a depositor withdraws after the stake has been committed, the pool's token balance drops below the amount it has staked. When the stake is later refunded to the pool, the remaining depositors' accounting (`depositBalance`) may not match the actual token balance, and the withdrawing depositor effectively steals from the remaining depositors' eventual refund.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deposits into the pool. 2. Pool reaches required stake and `createAssertion`/`createEdge` is called, committing the stake. 3. Attacker calls `withdrawFromPool` to pull their deposit back out. 4. The pool now holds less than the staked amount; when the stake is refunded, the pool's balance is less than the sum of remaining `depositBalance` entries, so later withdrawers cannot all be paid.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the staking pool; later depositors cannot withdraw their full balance; loss of funds for honest depositors.
hypotheses.recommendation: Prevent withdrawals once the stake has been committed (track a "committed" flag), or only allow withdrawal of the excess above the required stake.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder.onGasSpent double-refunds same tx via reentrant call
hypotheses.description: `onGasSpent` measures `gasUsed` from `startGasLeft` captured at entry, but it also calls `refundee.call{value: refundAmount}("")` before emitting the refund event. A malicious refundee can re-enter `onGasSpent` during that call (since `allowedContracts[msg.sender]` is whatever caller allowed), and the inner invocation sees the same `tx.gasprice`/`block.basefee` and measures fresh `startGasLeft`, computing a second refund from the same transaction. The function does not include the refund transfer’s own gas in `gasUsed` (it just adds a static `extraGasMargin`), so both inner and outer computations can significantly over-refund the actual `tx.gasprice * gasUsed`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker becomes an allowed refundee (or uses an allowed refundee address that forwards to a contract it controls). 2) Attacker is an allowed contract (e.g., a batch poster whose contract is allowed) that calls `onGasSpent` once per tx with `tx.gasprice` set at the cap. 3) The refundee is a contract whose fallback re-enters `onGasSpent` repeatedly until the refunder’s balance is drained. 4) Each reentry recomputes `gasUsed` from its own `startGasLeft`, and the refund amounts stack because there is no idempotency key per tx.
hypotheses.impact: GasRefunder balance is drained faster than the real gas cost of any single batch submission. Since the refunder is funded by protocol fees, this is direct loss of protocol funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the current refunded tx via `tx.origin`/nonce (or an explicit refundId) and forbid multiple refunds per refundId in the same block; or ignore reentrant calls by checking `msg.sender`/call depth and gating on a per-tx nonce.

hypotheses.title: RollupCreator receive() allows anyone to seed ETH used later by deployFactoriesToL2
hypotheses.description: `receive() external payable {}` lets anyone send ETH to the creator. `_deployFactories` refunds the entire `address(this).balance` to `msg.sender` after paying costs, and calls `l2FactoriesDeployer.perform{value: cost}`. Since `cost` is derived from the inbox/view functions rather than actual balance, an attacker can pre-seed the creator contract so that when a legitimate `createRollup` runs with `deployFactoriesToL2`, the refund includes the attacker's seed to the caller (the attacker if they are the caller). Not a direct theft from the caller since they pay the cost, but balances can be siphoned by an attacker who front-runs and calls `createRollup` with `deployFactoriesToL2=true` if the owner-seeded balance exists.
hypotheses.attackPath: If the owner or others have incidentally sent ETH to the creator, an attacker calls `createRollup` with `deployFactoriesToL2 = true` and ETH equal to (cost - any leftover balance) so that `address(this).balance` after paying `cost` includes the leftover, then the entire `address(this).balance` is refunded to the attacker's `msg.sender`.
hypotheses.impact: The attacker captures any ETH previously sitting in the creator contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track internal accounting for retryable funds or refund only the exact paid amount instead of `address(this).balance`.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder refunds more than gas actually spent due to gasleft accounting
hypotheses.description: The refund amount is computed as `estGasPrice * gasUsed` where `gasUsed` is derived from `startGasLeft + extraGasMargin + calldataCost*calldataSize - gasleft()`. Because `startGasLeft` is captured at the very beginning of the function and `gasleft()` is measured after several storage reads and branches, the measured `gasUsed` includes the cost of the refund logic itself, and the `extraGasMargin` (4000) plus calldata cost is added on top. This over-counts gas relative to what the caller actually spent on the refunded operation, so the refundee can receive more ETH than the gas they actually paid.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker becomes an allowed refundee (or is a legitimate one). 2. Attacker calls an allowed contract that invokes `onGasSpent` with a large `calldataSize` and a gas price near `maxGasCost`. 3. The formula adds `extraGasMargin` and `calldataSize * calldataCost` on top of the measured gas, and the measured gas already includes the refund function's own overhead. 4. Attacker receives a refund larger than the actual gas cost of the operation, draining the refunder's ETH balance over repeated calls.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of ETH from the GasRefunder contract; the refunder can be drained faster than intended, and the accounting of "gas spent" does not match real gas usage.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure gas usage more precisely (e.g., capture gasleft() immediately before the external call being refunded, or subtract the refund function's own overhead) and cap the refund at the actual gas cost paid by the caller.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder refunds gasUsed computed with attacker-influenced calldataSize
hypotheses.description: The `calldataSize` parameter is supplied by the calling contract (`msg.sender`), which is an allowed contract but the value is not verified against `msg.data.length`. An allowed contract (or a contract that becomes allowed) can pass an arbitrarily large `calldataSize` to inflate `gasUsed` via `calldataSize * calldataCost`, increasing the refund amount beyond actual gas spent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets a contract allowed (or exploits an allowed contract that forwards attacker-controlled calldataSize). 2) Calls `onGasSpent(refundee, gasUsed, hugeCalldataSize)`. 3) `gasUsed` is inflated by `hugeCalldataSize * 12`, and the refund is `estGasPrice * inflatedGasUsed`. 4) Attacker receives more ETH than the actual gas cost.
hypotheses.impact: Over-refund drains GasRefunder balance; loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ignore the caller-supplied `calldataSize` and use `msg.data.length` or verify it matches.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder.onGasSpent reentrancy via refundee callback
hypotheses.description: The refundee is paid via a low-level `call` before the function returns, and the contract's balance is read at the start of the function. A malicious refundee contract can reenter `onGasSpent` (or other functions) during the refund call, since the balance check `ownBalance` is computed before the external call and no reentrancy guard exists. The refundee is only required to be in `allowedRefundees`, but that mapping can include contracts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gets an address added to `allowedRefundees` (or is already allowed). 2) Attacker calls a whitelisted contract that invokes `onGasSpent` with the attacker's contract as refundee. 3) During the `refundee.call{value: refundAmount}("")`, the attacker's fallback reenters `onGasSpent` with the same or another allowed contract, draining additional refunds before the outer call completes. 4) Each nested call sees the same `ownBalance` snapshot logic and can pay out again.
hypotheses.impact: Multiple refunds paid out for a single gas expenditure, draining the GasRefunder balance faster than intended and potentially causing insolvency for legitimate refunds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard) to `onGasSpent`, or use a pull-payment pattern where refundees withdraw funds separately.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder refunds gas to arbitrary refundee without signature
hypotheses.description: `onGasSpent` is callable by any allowed contract and pays out ETH to any `refundee` that is in `allowedRefundees`. There is no signature, nonce, or binding between the caller (msg.sender) and the refundee, so any allowed contract can drain the refunder's balance by repeatedly calling `onGasSpent` with an allowed refundee address. The only limits are `maxSingleGasUsage` and `maxRefundeeBalance`, which are per-call and per-balance, not per-tx.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys/controls an allowed contract (or finds one that calls `onGasSpent` with attacker-supplied refundee). 2. Attacker calls `onGasSpent(attackerEOA, hugeGasUsed, hugeCalldataSize)` repeatedly. 3. Each call pays out up to `maxSingleGasUsage * estGasPrice` to the attacker EOA. 4. Repeat until the refunder's balance is drained.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of all ETH held by GasRefunder; other users' gas refunds fail.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the refundee to be the tx.origin or msg.sender, or require a signed authorization binding refundee, gasUsed, and a nonce.

hypotheses.title: RollupCreator.createRollup refunds entire balance to msg.sender
hypotheses.description: When `_nativeToken == address(0)`, `_deployFactories` sends `address(this).balance` to `msg.sender` after paying retryable costs. If the contract holds any pre-existing ETH (e.g. from a prior `receive()` or leftover refunds), the caller receives all of it. Conversely, if the caller underfunds, the call reverts and any ETH sent is stuck until another caller triggers a refund.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes RollupCreator holds ETH (from prior deposits or refunds). 2) Attacker calls `createRollup` with `deployFactoriesToL2=true` and `nativeToken=address(0)`, paying only the minimum required. 3) The contract refunds `address(this).balance` (including the pre-existing ETH) to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of any ETH held by RollupCreator; also griefing where a caller's ETH is trapped if a later step reverts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Refund only the excess paid by the caller (track `msg.value` minus actual cost), not `address(this).balance`.

hypotheses.title: EdgeStakingPool refund path missing; refundStake is not called by pool, funds stuck
hypotheses.description: `EdgeStakingPool` calls `EdgeChallengeManager.createLayerZeroEdge` once `stakeAmounts[args.level]` is approved. Unlike `AssertionStakingPool`, the pool exposes no function that calls `EdgeChallengeManager.refundStake(edgeId)`; the doc-comment for `EdgeStakingPool` states there is no need for such a function because `refundStake` exists, but `refundStake` is permissionless-because-anyone-but-sends-the-stake-to-`edge.staker`. Since `edge.staker` is the pool (created via `createLayerZeroEdge` from the pool’s context), the stake is transferred to the pool address, but there is no `IRollupUser(rollup).withdrawStakerFunds()`-style unlock path in the pool that calls `refundStake`. Meaningful amounts can be lost because `withdrawFromPool` has no record of the added edge stake.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Users deposit into an EdgeStakingPool. 2) Pool creates the layer-zero edge, locking stake in the challenge manager under staker address = pool. 3) After the edge is confirmed, an external actor (anyone) must call `refundStake(edgeId)` to push the tokens to the pool. 4) The pool has no code to invoke `refundStake` and no hook when it is called; if an attacker front-runs the refund and the tokens arrive while the pool is still awaiting other accounting, the contract has no refund reconciliation and depositors may race each other for fixed `depositBalance` beyond available tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Refunded stake sits idle in the pool with no function to invoke `refundStake` (see `EdgeStakingPool.sol`), unless an external caller invokes it — the pool itself never triggers this, so stake remains in the challenge manager until an unrelated actor chooses to call it. Once it is called, token arrival competes with fixed per-user withdraw balances, mirroring the AbsBoldStakingPool finding above.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `refundStakeToPool()` function calling `EdgeChallengeManager(challengeManager).refundStake(edgeId)`; and after tokens return, disallow withdrawals only against `min(contractBalance, sumOfDeposits)` to keep pro-rata semantics.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder refunds to arbitrary refundee without checking msg.sender is the refundee
hypotheses.description: `onGasSpent` accepts an arbitrary `refundee` address from the caller (the allowed contract) and sends ETH to it. The function only checks `allowedContracts[msg.sender]` and `allowedRefundees[refundee]`, but does not verify that the refundee is the actual party that paid gas. Any allowed contract can direct refunds to any allowed refundee, and the refund amount is computed from `tx.gasprice` and `gasUsed` supplied by the caller, allowing the caller to inflate `calldataSize`/`gasUsed` up to `maxSingleGasUsage`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls or compromises an allowed contract (or is an allowed contract). 2) Calls `onGasSpent(attackerControlledAllowedRefundee, hugeGasUsed, hugeCalldataSize)` with a high `tx.gasprice`. 3) The function computes `refundAmount = estGasPrice * gasUsed` capped only by `maxSingleGasUsage` and `ownBalance`, then sends ETH to the attacker's refundee. 4) Repeat until the contract's balance is drained.
hypotheses.impact: Drain of GasRefunder ETH balance; loss of funds intended for legitimate gas refunds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `refundee == tx.origin` (or the actual gas payer) and/or bind refunds to the caller's own gas usage rather than caller-supplied values.

hypotheses.title: EdgeChallengeManager initializer callable by anyone on implementation
hypotheses.description: `EdgeChallengeManager` inherits `Initializable` and calls `_disableInitializers()` in the constructor, but the challenge manager `IMPL_CHALLENGE_MANAGER` is used as a template behind a `TransparentUpgradeableProxy` created by `BOLDUpgradeAction`. In `RollupCreator.createChallengeManager` and `BOLDUpgradeAction.perform`, the proxy is deployed and immediately initialized in the same tx, but if any deployment path leaves the proxy uninitialized (or if the implementation is deployed without `_disableInitializers` being invoked through the constructor path being bypassed), an attacker can front-run initialization of a fresh proxy.
hypotheses.attackPath: If a proxy is created without initializing in the same transaction (e.g. via `new TransparentUpgradeableProxy(...)`), the attacker observes the deployment and calls `initialize` with attacker-controlled `_excessStakeReceiver`, `_stakeToken`, `_assertionChain` and stake amounts, taking control of staking configuration and excess stake routing.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker becomes the `excessStakeReceiver` and can set arbitrary `assertionChain`/`stakeToken`/stake amounts, causing loss of stake refunds and incorrect challenge validation for the whole rollup.
hypotheses.recommendation: Always initialize the proxy in the same transaction as deployment (RollupCreator already does), and confirm the logic contract is `_disableInitializers`-protected; alternatively add an `onlyDelegated`-style guard for template initialization.

hypotheses.title: AssertionStakingPool.createAssertion can be called repeatedly draining pool allowance
hypotheses.description: `createAssertion` calls `safeIncreaseAllowance(rollup, requiredStake)` and then `newStakeOnNewAssertion`. There is no check that the pool has not already created the assertion, nor that the pool's balance is sufficient beyond what the rollup enforces. If the pool has excess deposits (the contract explicitly allows total deposits to exceed required stake), a caller can call `createAssertion` multiple times as long as the rollup accepts new stakes. Each call increases the allowance and stakes again, potentially locking more of the pool's tokens than intended and leaving depositors unable to withdraw.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Depositors fund the pool beyond the required stake. 2. Attacker calls `createAssertion` once (succeeds). 3. Attacker calls `createAssertion` again; if the rollup allows a new stake (e.g., after the first assertion is confirmed or if the pool is not yet staked), the pool stakes again. 4. Pool tokens are locked in the rollup, and depositors cannot withdraw their full balances.
hypotheses.impact: Pool funds locked in the rollup beyond the intended single stake; depositors cannot withdraw; potential loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track whether the pool has already created the assertion and revert on subsequent calls; also cap the allowance to the exact required stake.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder refunds based on tx.gasprice without verifying actual gas paid
hypotheses.description: The refund amount is computed as `estGasPrice * gasUsed` where `estGasPrice` is derived from `block.basefee + maxGasTip` capped by `tx.gasprice` and `maxGasCost`. Because `tx.gasprice` is attacker-controlled (the caller sets it), a refundee can set an arbitrarily high `tx.gasprice` up to `maxGasCost` to inflate the refund, even if the actual effective gas price paid is lower (e.g., via EIP-1559 where basefee is much lower than maxFeePerGas). The contract pays out `estGasPrice * gasUsed` in ETH regardless of what was actually paid.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker becomes an allowed refundee (or colludes with one). 2) Attacker submits a tx with `maxFeePerGas` set to `maxGasCost` (120 gwei) but actual basefee is low. 3) `tx.gasprice` returns the effective gas price which can be near maxFeePerGas if basefee is high, but more importantly the attacker can set `maxPriorityFeePerGas` high to push `tx.gasprice` up. 4) The refund is computed at the inflated `estGasPrice`, draining the GasRefunder balance faster than actual gas costs.
hypotheses.impact: GasRefunder balance drained faster than intended; loss of funds from the refunder contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `tx.gasprice` directly (which is the effective gas price) rather than `block.basefee + maxGasTip`, or cap refunds to the actual gas cost paid by the tx.

hypotheses.title: RollupCreator refunds excess ETH to msg.sender without reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: `_deployFactories` sends `address(this).balance` to `msg.sender` via a low-level call after performing retryable ticket creation. If `msg.sender` is a contract, it can reenter `createRollup` (which is `payable` and public) and cause the refund to be sent again, or manipulate the balance accounting. The refund amount is the entire contract balance, not just the excess from this call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker contract calls `createRollup` with `deployFactoriesToL2=true` and `nativeToken=address(0)`. 2. During the refund call, attacker reenters `createRollup` with a smaller msg.value. 3. The second call's refund sends the remaining balance to the attacker again.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can drain any ETH that other users sent to RollupCreator (e.g., for other rollup creations) or that was left over.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the exact excess amount and refund only that, and add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: RollupCreator.createRollup refund call reentrancy before state finalization
hypotheses.description: In `_deployFactories`, when `_nativeToken == address(0)`, the contract refunds the caller via `msg.sender.call{value: address(this).balance}("")` after `l2FactoriesDeployer.perform`. The refund is sent before `createRollup` returns and before the `RollupCreated` event is emitted. A malicious caller contract can reenter `createRollup` during the refund callback, potentially creating multiple rollups with the same salt or manipulating the refund amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that calls `createRollup` with `deployFactoriesToL2 = true` and `nativeToken = address(0)`. 2) During the refund `call`, the attacker's fallback reenters `createRollup` with the same `deployParams` (same salt). 3) The second call may succeed or revert depending on state, but the attacker can attempt to extract additional refunds or cause inconsistent state. 4) The attacker can also reenter to drain any ETH held by RollupCreator.
hypotheses.impact: Potential double-refund or draining of ETH held by RollupCreator, and inconsistent rollup creation state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a reentrancy guard on `createRollup`, or use `transfer`/`send` with a pull-payment pattern for refunds.

hypotheses.title: ValidatorWallet.executeTransactionsWithGasRefunder reentrancy via destination call
hypotheses.description: The function loops over destinations and performs low-level `call` to each. If a destination is a malicious contract, it can reenter `executeTransactionsWithGasRefunder` or `executeTransactionWithGasRefunder` during the call. The `onlyExecutorOrOwner` modifier allows executors (which may be contracts) to call, and `validateExecuteTransaction` only checks `allowedExecutorDestinations`. A malicious destination can reenter and execute additional transactions.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is an executor or owner (or compromises one). 2) Attacker calls `executeTransactionsWithGasRefunder` with a malicious destination contract. 3) During the `call`, the destination reenters `executeTransactionsWithGasRefunder` with additional destinations/amounts. 4) The attacker can execute arbitrary transactions beyond the intended batch, potentially draining the wallet.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized transactions executed from the ValidatorWallet, potentially draining ETH or calling arbitrary contracts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `executeTransactionsWithGasRefunder` and `executeTransactionWithGasRefunder`.

hypotheses.title: EdgeChallengeManager.multiUpdateTimeCacheByChildren unbounded loop
hypotheses.description: `multiUpdateTimeCacheByChildren` loops over a user-supplied `edgeIds` array with no bound. Each iteration performs storage reads/writes and emits events. A caller can supply a very large array, causing the transaction to run out of gas. While the caller pays the gas, this can be used to grief if the function is called by a contract that expects it to succeed, or if it is used in a batch that must complete.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `multiUpdateTimeCacheByChildren` with a huge array of edge IDs. 2) The transaction consumes all gas and reverts. 3) If any on-chain logic depends on this call succeeding (e.g. a keeper), it is blocked.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing of keepers or automated systems that rely on this function; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a maximum array length or process in chunks.

hypotheses.title: AssertionStakingPool allows depositors to withdraw after assertion posted, leaving protocol underfunded
hypotheses.description: `depositIntoPool` records `depositBalance[msg.sender]` but the pool only transfers the actual stake to the rollup/edge manager when `createAssertion`/`createEdge` is called. Once the assertion/edge is posted, the pool’s share of stake is locked in the target protocol, but the contract has no accounting that prevents depositors from `withdrawFromPool`. The doc-comment claims "any depositor can withdraw some stake early even after the protocol move has been made... all depositors will still be eventually refunded", but if the target protocol has already consumed the stake (or the assertion loses and only the `loserStakeEscrow` address is refunded), `withdrawFromPool` will revert/underflow only when the contract is empty — earlier depositors get paid, later depositors do not.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Depositor deposits just enough to push the pool over `requiredStake` via someone else’s deposit. 2) Another user calls `createAssertion`/`createEdge`, moving the multi-user stake to the rollup/edge manager. 3) Attacker front-runs any subsequent refund and calls `withdrawFromPool()` for their full `depositBalance`. 4) If the assertion is later disputed and only a fraction is returned, the pool is short and the remaining depositors cannot be repaid.
hypotheses.impact: Fair-share refund distribution is violated; last-in depositors lose funds, first-out depositors profit. If the assertion loses entirely, the entire pool balance may be lost to `loserStakeEscrow` while early withdrawers already exited.
hypotheses.recommendation: Disallow withdrawals once `createAssertion`/`createEdge` has been called and only re-enable after the returned stake has been reconciled to `totalDeposited` in a pro-rata way; otherwise restrict withdrawals to `min(depositBalance, contractBalance* share)` after stake is returned.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder refunds to refundee even when call fails, no revert handling
hypotheses.description: The function performs `refundee.call{value: refundAmount}("")` and stores the result in `success`, but does not revert or adjust accounting if the call fails. The event is emitted with `success=false` but the ETH is not returned to the contract's accounting (it stays in the contract if the call failed, but the function returns `success` which is false). More importantly, the function returns `success` which is the result of the ETH transfer, not whether the refund was granted. Callers relying on the return value may misinterpret a failed ETH transfer as a denied refund.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A refundee that is a contract with a reverting receive() function is allowed. 2. The allowed contract calls onGasSpent. 3. The ETH transfer fails, `success` is false, but the function returns false without reverting. 4. The caller may treat this as a denial and retry, or the ETH remains stuck in the refunder.
hypotheses.impact: ETH can become stuck in the GasRefunder if the refundee cannot receive ETH; the return value semantics are ambiguous.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if the ETH transfer fails, or explicitly handle the failure by not consuming the refund and returning a clear status.

hypotheses.title: EdgeStakingPool.createEdge can be called repeatedly staking multiple times
hypotheses.description: Similar to AssertionStakingPool, `createEdge` calls `safeIncreaseAllowance` and `createLayerZeroEdge` without tracking whether the edge has already been created. If the pool holds excess deposits, a caller can call `createEdge` multiple times, each time staking the required amount from the pool. The challenge manager will reject duplicate edge IDs, but the allowance increase and the attempt still consume gas and, more importantly, if the edge ID check passes on a different edge (or if the pool is reused), multiple stakes can be locked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Depositors over-fund the pool. 2. Attacker calls `createEdge` with valid args; edge is created and stake is locked. 3. Attacker calls `createEdge` again with args that produce a different edge ID (or the same, causing revert but after allowance increase). 4. Pool tokens are locked in the challenge manager, and depositors cannot withdraw.
hypotheses.impact: Pool funds locked beyond the intended single stake; depositors cannot withdraw; potential loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track whether the edge has already been created and revert on subsequent calls; cap the allowance to the exact required stake.

hypotheses.title: RollupUserLogic.stakeOnNewAssertion sends requiredStake to loserStakeEscrow without checking excess
hypotheses.description: When a staker creates a non-first-child assertion, the code transfers `assertion.beforeStateData.configData.requiredStake` to `loserStakeEscrow`. However, the staker may have staked more than `requiredStake` (the code explicitly notes "the staker may have more than enough stake, and the entire stake will be locked"). The excess stake is not accounted for and remains locked on the losing assertion, effectively lost to the staker. The comment acknowledges this but it is still an accounting flaw where the protocol takes more than the required stake from the losing staker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Staker stakes more than `requiredStake` (e.g., via `addToDeposit`). 2. Staker creates a non-first-child assertion. 3. The full `requiredStake` is sent to `loserStakeEscrow`, but the staker's excess remains locked on the losing assertion. 4. The staker cannot recover the excess.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of excess stake for the losing staker; funds effectively frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only transfer the exact `requiredStake` and refund or account for the excess, or document and enforce that stakers cannot stake more than `requiredStake`.

hypotheses.title: Inbox.calculateRetryableSubmissionFee uses block.basefee when baseFee=0
hypotheses.description: When `baseFee == 0`, the function falls back to `block.basefee`. This is used by `_unsafeCreateRetryableTicket` to compute `submissionFee` and compare against `maxSubmissionCost`. If `block.basefee` is manipulated (e.g., via a miner/validator on L1, or on an L2 host chain where basefee can be influenced), the required submission fee changes. More importantly, `DeployHelper.getDeploymentTotalCost` calls this with `block.basefee` explicitly, so the cost is computed at the current basefee, but the actual retryable is submitted later — a basefee spike between quote and execution causes underfunding.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `createRollup` with `deployFactoriesToL2=true`. 2) Attacker (as a sequencer/miner on the host chain, or via basefee manipulation) spikes `block.basefee`. 3) The retryable submission fee computed inside `_unsafeCreateRetryableTicket` exceeds `maxSubmissionCost`, causing the retryable to revert or the ticket to be underfunded.
hypotheses.impact: Rollup creation with factory deployment can fail or factories not deployed, breaking deterministic addresses.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require an explicit non-zero `baseFee` parameter or add a buffer to `maxSubmissionCost`.

hypotheses.title: SequencerInbox blob gas cost uses block.basefee without staleness check
hypotheses.description: The blob cost is computed as `reader4844.getBlobBaseFee() * GAS_PER_BLOB * dataHashes.length` and then divided by `block.basefee` to normalize to gas units. If `block.basefee` is zero (possible on some L2 host chains or during edge cases), the ternary returns 0, meaning the batch poster gets no spending report credit for blob gas. Conversely, if `block.basefee` is manipulated, the normalized `extraGas` is wrong, leading to incorrect batch posting refunds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (batch poster) submits a blob batch when `block.basefee` is very low. 2) The normalized `extraGas` becomes very large (blobCost / tiny basefee), potentially exceeding `type(uint64).max` and reverting with `ExtraGasNotUint64`, or being capped incorrectly. 3) Batch posting refund is miscomputed.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect batch posting refund accounting; potential DoS of blob batch submission.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a more robust normalization or cap `extraGas` before the division.

hypotheses.title: RollupUserLogic.stakeOnNewAssertion token transfer before state update
hypotheses.description: In `stakeOnNewAssertion`, when the new assertion is not the first child, `IERC20(stakeToken).safeTransfer(loserStakeEscrow, requiredStake)` is called. If `stakeToken` is an ERC777-style token with transfer hooks, the `loserStakeEscrow` (or the token itself) can reenter the rollup. The state update `_stakerMap[msg.sender].latestStakedAssertion = newAssertionHash` occurs before the transfer, but other state (e.g., assertion status, staker balances) may be inconsistent during the callback.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a malicious ERC20 token as `stakeToken` (if the rollup is configured with such a token) or exploits a token with hooks. 2) Attacker calls `stakeOnNewAssertion` with a non-first-child assertion. 3) During `safeTransfer` to `loserStakeEscrow`, the token invokes a hook on `loserStakeEscrow` (if it's a contract) or on the attacker. 4) The attacker reenters `stakeOnNewAssertion` or other functions, potentially creating multiple assertions or manipulating staker state.
hypotheses.impact: Potential double-spending of stake, incorrect staker accounting, or assertion state corruption.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a reentrancy guard on `stakeOnNewAssertion`, or ensure `stakeToken` cannot have transfer hooks (as documented in ERC20Bridge).

hypotheses.title: AbsBoldStakingPool.withdrawFromPool state update before transfer
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFromPool` updates `depositBalance[msg.sender]` before calling `IERC20(stakeToken).safeTransfer(msg.sender, amount)`. If `stakeToken` has transfer hooks (e.g., ERC777), the recipient can reenter `withdrawFromPool` or `depositIntoPool`. The state update before the transfer mitigates double-withdrawal, but reentrancy into `depositIntoPool` could manipulate balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits into the pool. 2) Attacker calls `withdrawFromPool` with a token that has a transfer hook. 3) During the `safeTransfer`, the attacker's hook reenters `depositIntoPool` or `withdrawFromPool`. 4) The attacker can potentially manipulate their balance or the pool's token balance.
hypotheses.impact: Potential incorrect balance accounting or token drainage if the token has hooks.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `withdrawFromPool` and `depositIntoPool`, or restrict `stakeToken` to non-hook tokens.

hypotheses.title: RollupUserLogic.withdrawStakerFunds reverts on zero, blocking withdrawals
hypotheses.description: `withdrawStakerFunds` requires `amount > 0` and reverts with `NO_FUNDS_TO_WITHDRAW` otherwise. If a staker's withdrawable funds are zero (e.g. after a partial withdrawal or because their stake was moved), any call reverts. More importantly, if the stake token is a token that reverts on zero-value transfers, or if accounting leaves a user with zero, the function cannot be used to clear state.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an attacker; it is a liveness issue where a user with zero withdrawable funds cannot call the function, but this is expected. The real risk is if `withdrawFunds` returns zero due to a prior partial withdrawal and the user is stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Users with zero withdrawable balance cannot call the function, but this is by design. Low impact.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow zero withdrawals or return early without reverting.

hypotheses.title: AbsBoldStakingPool.withdrawFromPool reverts on zero amount
hypotheses.description: `withdrawFromPool(uint256 amount)` reverts if `amount == 0`. The no-arg overload calls `withdrawFromPool(depositBalance[msg.sender])`, so a user with zero balance cannot call it. This is a minor liveness issue but could block automated flows that call the no-arg version unconditionally.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user with zero deposit calls `withdrawFromPool()` and reverts; no funds lost, but any contract integrating this and calling unconditionally will revert.
hypotheses.impact: Minor: integrations that call `withdrawFromPool()` unconditionally will revert for zero-balance users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Return early if amount is zero instead of reverting.

hypotheses.title: SequencerInbox.forceInclusion can be blocked by buffer depletion
hypotheses.description: `forceInclusion` requires `l1BlockAndTime[0] + delayBlocks_ < block.number`. When `isDelayBufferable` is true, `delayBlocks_` is set to `delayBufferableBlocks(buffer.bufferBlocks)`, which can be as low as `buffer.bufferBlocks`. If the buffer is depleted (e.g. by a malicious sequencer posting many delayed messages), `delayBlocks_` becomes very small, making it easier to force include. However, the buffer can also be replenished, and if the buffer is full, `delayBlocks_` equals `delayBlocks`. The real issue is that `buffer.update` is called with `l1BlockAndTime[0]`, which is user-supplied. An attacker can supply a very old `l1BlockAndTime[0]` to manipulate the buffer update, potentially causing the buffer to be depleted or replenished incorrectly, blocking force inclusion.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `forceInclusion` with a crafted `l1BlockAndTime[0]` that is very old. 2) `buffer.update` is called with this old block number, which may cause the buffer to be updated incorrectly (e.g. replenished too much or depleted). 3) This can make `delayBlocks_` large, preventing force inclusion of legitimate delayed messages.
hypotheses.impact: Delayed messages cannot be force-included, allowing the sequencer to censor users indefinitely.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `l1BlockAndTime[0]` is not too old or use `block.number` for buffer updates.

hypotheses.title: Inbox fork functions lack chain-id binding in signed payload
hypotheses.description: The fork-related functions (`sendL1FundedUnsignedTransactionToFork`, `sendUnsignedTransactionToFork`, `sendWithdrawEthToFork`) build an L2 unsigned transaction payload containing `nonce`, `gasLimit`, `maxFeePerGas`, `to`, `value`, and `data`, but do not include the L1 chain id or the target rollup address in the signed/encoded payload. If the same L1 fork is replayed on a different chain (or the same chain after a reorg), the same payload can be re-submitted and executed again on L2 because the L2 nonce is the only replay protection and it is per-L2-account, not per-L1-chain.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a fork transaction on chain A. 2. Attacker replays the same calldata on chain B (or after a reorg on chain A) where the same L1 inbox is deployed. 3. The L2 message is delivered again; if the L2 account's nonce has not advanced (e.g., different L2 account or fresh state), the transaction executes.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate execution of fork transactions on L2, potentially double-spending value or repeating state changes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` and the inbox/rollup address in the encoded payload so the L2 can reject cross-chain replays.

hypotheses.title: SequencerInbox forceInclusion lacks chain-id binding in message hash
hypotheses.description: `forceInclusion` reconstructs the delayed message hash from user-supplied `kind`, `l1BlockAndTime`, `baseFeeL1`, `sender`, and `messageDataHash`, then verifies it against `bridge.delayedInboxAccs`. The message hash does not include the L1 chain id or the bridge address. If the same delayed message preimage is valid on two chains (e.g., after a fork), the same force-inclusion proof can be replayed on both chains.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a valid delayed message on chain A. 2. After a fork, the same message exists on chain B. 3. Attacker calls `forceInclusion` on chain B with the same parameters, including the message in chain B's inbox without the sequencer's consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized force-inclusion of delayed messages on a forked chain, potentially bypassing sequencer ordering.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` and the bridge address in `Messages.messageHash` or in the force-inclusion validation.

hypotheses.title: AbsOutbox executeTransaction lacks chain-id binding in item hash
hypotheses.description: `calculateItemHash` hashes `l2Sender, to, l2Block, l1Block, l2Timestamp, value, data` but does not include the L1 chain id or the outbox address. If the same L2-to-L1 message is included in two different L1 chains (e.g., after a fork), the same proof and parameters can be replayed on both chains, executing the L1 call twice.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a valid L2-to-L1 withdrawal on chain A. 2. After a fork, the same send root exists on chain B. 3. Attacker calls `executeTransaction` on chain B with the same proof and parameters, executing the withdrawal again.
hypotheses.impact: Double execution of L2-to-L1 messages, potentially draining funds from L1 contracts that trust the outbox.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` and the outbox address in `calculateItemHash`.

hypotheses.title: EdgeChallengeManager refundStake lacks replay protection across chains
hypotheses.description: `refundStake` marks an edge as refunded and transfers the stake to `edge.staker`. The edge id is computed from `level, originId, startHeight, startHistoryRoot, endHeight, endHistoryRoot`, none of which include the L1 chain id or the challenge manager address. If the same edge is created on two chains (e.g., after a fork), the same edge id can be refunded on both chains, but the stake token is per-chain so this is only a problem if the same token is bridged.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker creates an edge on chain A and gets it confirmed. 2. After a fork, the same edge exists on chain B. 3. Attacker calls `refundStake` on chain B, receiving a second refund.
hypotheses.impact: Double refund of stake, draining the challenge manager's stake token balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid` and the challenge manager address in the edge id computation.

hypotheses.title: Submit batch spending report recorded on every batch, enabling repeated L1->L2 refunds to same batch poster
hypotheses.description: `submitBatchSpendingReport` is called in `addSequencerL2BatchImpl` for every batch that has `calldataLengthPosted > 0` while `isUsingFeeToken == false`, and again from `addSequencerL2BatchFromBlobsImpl`. The report is a delayed message that (per the code’s comment) credits `tx.origin` for the gas cost on L2. There is no uniqueness/dedup constraint keyed to the batch: as long as a batch poster is set and a batch is enqueued, a fresh spending report is enqueued, so a single batch poster address (or an attacker who registers batch posters and batch poster manager) can repeatedly trigger batches and collect the "spending report" credit on L2 without the L2-side accounting tying it uniquely to a single delivered data hash.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is authorized as a batch poster (rollup owner added them, but this is an untrusted external role in the deployment). 2) Attacker submits an empty/zero-data batch repeatedly with `afterDelayedMessagesRead` incrementing only on a no-op, or submits many small batches via `addSequencerL2BatchFromCalldataImpl` with valid flags. 3) Each call emits a `SequencerBatchDelivered` and a `submitBatchSpendingReport`, which enqueues a delayed message that composes into the L2 gas refund accounting. 4) On L2, the batch poster is credited for each of these reports even though the L1 gas was shared or trivial.
hypotheses.impact: Steady leakage of L2-refundable fees to the batch poster address on every batch. Because the L2 refund amount is separate from the actual gas paid per batch report message, the credit per batch is not bounded by the actual L1 gas spent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Aggregate batch spending reports (e.g., one report per tx via a per-tx `reportSubmitted` flag, keyed by `tx.origin`), or require the report to consume gas proportional to the reported spending.

hypotheses.title: AssertionStakingPool.createAssertion can be front-run to steal pool-funded assertion stake reward path
hypotheses.description: `createAssertion` reads `requiredStake` from the caller-supplied `assertionInputs.beforeStateData.configData.requiredStake` and then calls `IRollupUser(rollup).newStakeOnNewAssertion(requiredStake, assertionInputs, assertionHash, address(this))`, all from the pool’s context but with the pool as the staker. However, `assertionInputs` (including `afterState`, `beforeState`, config, etc.) are also caller-supplied, while the on-chain linkage between the supplied `assertionHash` and the actual created assertion is only validated inside the rollup via `expectedAssertionHash`. Because the pool stores `assertionHash` as immutable, but the pool does not check that the deposited tokens are only released to `requiredStake` for the *intended* assertion (`assertionHash` is just passed through), an attacker can deploy the pool, deposit the minimum, then call `createAssertion` with `assertionInputs` whose `beforeStateData.configData.requiredStake` is much larger than what they deposited (funded by other depositors) — the rollup will accept as soon as enough stake is present, and the attacker gets to create the assertion that earns the eventual stake-refund / validator reward on confirmation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates an `AssertionStakingPool` for a target `assertionHash`. 2) Honest users deposit; the pool reaches or exceeds `requiredStake`. 3) Attacker front-runs by calling `createAssertion` with `assertionInputs` that pass `newStakeOnNewAssertion` and set the staker to `address(this)` (pool). 4) The assertion posts, tokens are locked; the attacker retains `withdrawalAddress = address(this)` in the staker record, so the eventual refund goes back into the pool where the attacker can pull proportionally more than what they contributed (they deposited the minimum).
hypotheses.impact: Attackers who deposit the minimum share the victory/reward benefits proportional to their share only, but the risk/cost of posting the assertion has been paid by honest depositors who could otherwise have been the ones to post. In the worst case, attackers who can replay this quickly across pools get a systematic unfair advantage, and honest users lose the ability to count as the asserting party.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind `requiredStake` to the pool’s stored `assertionHash` (compute/verify it in the pool, do not trust the caller-supplied config) and record the creator of the assertion so that refunds are attributed fairly among depositors.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Inbox approves bridge with max allowance indefinitely
hypotheses.description: `initialize` sets `IERC20(nativeToken).approve(address(bridge), type(uint256).max)`. This leaves an unlimited, permanent allowance from the Inbox to the Bridge. If the bridge address is ever changed or the bridge implementation is upgraded to a malicious/buggy version, the bridge can drain all native tokens held by the Inbox (including user funds in transit for retryables).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A future bridge upgrade (or a compromised bridge) calls `transferFrom(inbox, attacker, balance)` on the native token. 2) Because the Inbox granted max allowance, the transfer succeeds. 3) Attacker drains all native tokens held by the Inbox.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of all native tokens held by the Inbox; user funds in transit for retryable tickets are stolen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Approve only the exact amount needed per transfer, or use a scoped allowance that is reset after each use.

hypotheses.title: AssertionStakingPool.createAssertion leaves open allowance to rollup
hypotheses.description: `createAssertion` calls `IERC20(stakeToken).safeIncreaseAllowance(rollup, requiredStake)` but never resets the allowance. If `newStakeOnNewAssertion` does not consume the full allowance (e.g., due to a revert path or a future rollup change), the residual allowance remains. More importantly, the pool holds user deposits and the rollup can pull up to `requiredStake` at any time via `transferFrom`, even outside the intended call.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A malicious or upgraded rollup (or a bug in the rollup) calls `transferFrom(pool, attacker, allowance)` on the stake token. 2) The pool's allowance to the rollup permits the transfer. 3) User deposits are drained.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user deposits held by the staking pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `safeApprove(rollup, requiredStake)` before the call and reset to 0 immediately after, or use a pull-based pattern.

hypotheses.title: EdgeStakingPool.createEdge leaves open allowance to challenge manager
hypotheses.description: `createEdge` calls `IERC20(stakeToken).safeIncreaseAllowance(address(challengeManager), requiredStake)` and never resets it. The pool holds user deposits; the challenge manager can pull up to `requiredStake` at any time via `transferFrom`, even outside the intended `createLayerZeroEdge` call. If the challenge manager is upgraded or has a bug, user deposits can be drained.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A malicious or upgraded challenge manager calls `transferFrom(pool, attacker, allowance)` on the stake token. 2) The pool's allowance permits the transfer. 3) User deposits are drained.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user deposits held by the staking pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reset the allowance to 0 after `createLayerZeroEdge`, or use a pull-based pattern.

hypotheses.title: GasRefunder disallower can be anyone set by owner, but disallow permits self through owner()
hypotheses.description: `disallowContracts` requires `msg.sender == owner() || msg.sender == disallower`. If `disallower` is set to `address(0)` (default), or if `disallower` is accidentally set to `address(this)`, the check degrades; but more importantly `disallower` can be set by the owner to any address, and there is no way to remove it except by overwriting. This is not attacker-reachable without owner action, so scope is limited.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not attacker-reachable; requires owner to set a malicious/compromised `disallower`.
hypotheses.impact: A compromised disallower can grief by disallowing contracts/refundees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an explicit `setDisallower(address(0))` removal path and emit events on change (already emitted).

hypotheses.title: SequencerInbox addSequencerL2Batch spoofable via rollup address as msg.sender
hypotheses.description: `addSequencerL2Batch` and `addSequencerL2BatchDelayProof` allow `msg.sender == address(rollup)` in addition to batch posters. Since `rollup` is the `RollupProxy` contract, arbitrary users cannot directly call it as the rollup, but if any function on the rollup is externally callable and performs a call to the sequencer inbox, an attacker could pivot. In practice the rollup does not call the sequencer inbox, so this is only a defense-in-depth concern.
hypotheses.attackPath: A crafted transaction sent to the rollup contract that has a fallback forwarding to the sequencer inbox could spoof batch posting; no such path exists in this codebase.
hypotheses.impact: Potential unauthorized batch posting if a forwarding path exists.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict to batch posters unless there is a specific need and use an explicit modifier.
